facts.fact_text: At noon on 5 August 2000, the applicants, together with thirty-nine others, gathered in İstiklal Street in Istanbul to make a press declaration to protest against F-type prisons.
The demonstrators attempted to march along İstiklal Street on 5 August 2000, chanting slogans and reading out a press declaration.
On 19 September 2005, the Beyoğlu Criminal Court acquitted the applicants.
The Beyoğlu Criminal Court held that making a press statement was a constitutional right and that prior authorisation was not needed to exercise this right.
The Beyoğlu Criminal Court concluded that the accused had used their constitutional rights and, consequently, had not committed any offence.
Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that everyone has the right to hold unarmed and peaceful meetings and demonstration marches without prior permission.

The applicants were arrested on 5 August 2000 along with thirty-nine other persons.
Following the events of 5 August 2000, the applicants were taken to Beyoğlu central police directorate, where they were kept for one day.
Following the events of 5 August 2000, the applicants were taken to Karaköy police station, where they were kept for one day.
On 14 August 2000, the Beyoğlu public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Beyoğlu Criminal Court against the applicants.
The Beyoğlu public prosecutor accused the applicants under Article 28 § 1 of Law No. 2911 (Assemblies and Marches Act) of taking part in an illegal demonstration without prior authorisation.
The Beyoğlu public prosecutor accused the applicants under Article 28 § 1 of Law No. 2911 (Assemblies and Marches Act) of not dispersing despite the police officers' warning.

In his decision of 5 January 2001, the Beyoğlu public prosecutor considered that the force used by the security forces was in line with Article 16 of Law No. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police.

Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that the formalities, conditions, and procedures governing the exercise of the right to hold meetings and demonstration marches shall be prescribed by law.

At the material time, section 10 of the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law No. 2911) required that, in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration was planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising board.

Section 22 of the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law No. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions on public streets, in parks, places of worship, and buildings in which public services were based.

Section 24 of the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provided that demonstrations and processions which did not comply with the provisions of that law would be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators had been warned.

Additional Article 6 (dated 16 June 1985) of Law No. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that in cases of resistance by persons whose arrest is necessary or by groups whose dispersal is necessary, or of their threatening to attack or carrying out an attack, the police may use violence to subdue these actions.

Additional Article 6 (dated 16 June 1985) of Law No. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that use of violence refers to the use of bodily force, physical force and all types of weapons specified in the law, and that it gradually increases according to the nature and level of resistance and attack in such a way as to restore calm.

Intelligence reports were received indicating that on 5 August 2000 a group of demonstrators would gather in İstiklal Street in Istanbul to read a press declaration and block the tram line to protest against F-type prisons.

Section 22 of the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law No. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions on public streets, in parks, places of worship, and buildings in which public services were based.

Section 22 of the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law No. 2911) required that demonstrations organised in public squares comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.
At noon on 5 August 2000, the applicants, together with thirty-nine others, gathered in İstiklal Street in Istanbul to make a press declaration to protest against F-type prisons.
The police asked the group gathered in İstiklal Street on 5 August 2000 to disperse and to end the gathering.
The police informed the group gathered in İstiklal Street on 5 August 2000 that the demonstration was unlawful since no advance notice had been submitted to the authorities.
At about 12.30 p.m. on 5 August 2000, the police dispersed the group gathered in İstiklal Street, allegedly by using truncheons and tear-gas.
The applicant Sema Gül was subsequently taken to the Taksim Hospital following the events of 5 August 2000.
The applicant Semiha Kırkoç was subsequently taken to the Taksim Hospital following the events of 5 August 2000.
The doctor who examined the applicant Sema Gül noted: 'There are bruises on both arms and a swelling on the left foot.'
The doctor who examined the applicant Semiha Kırkoç noted: 'There is a 4 cm long laceration on the left parietal region.'
The incident report dated 5 August 2000 stated that the security forces had to use force to disperse the group because the group refused to obey the warnings.
In his decision of 5 January 2001, the Beyoğlu public prosecutor considered that the force used by the security forces had not been excessive.
In his decision of 5 January 2001, the Beyoğlu public prosecutor opined that the injuries sustained by the complainants had been caused by the use of force which was proportionate.
On 19 September 2005, the Beyoğlu Criminal Court acquitted the applicants.
The Beyoğlu Criminal Court held that making a press statement was a constitutional right and that prior authorisation was not needed to exercise this right.
The Beyoğlu Criminal Court observed that it was not certain that the warning given to the accused to disperse could be heard by all the demonstrators.
The Beyoğlu Criminal Court concluded that the accused had used their constitutional rights and, consequently, had not committed any offence.
